articles.title: The prophetic word may depend more on the soil it lands in than on its own power
articles.deck: A prayer written through Luke 8, on the words God has spoken that have not happened yet, and the honest possibility that the delay is not his.

archiveMeta.editNote: Published as it appeared in the September 2013 issue, page 8. Column reading order repaired and typographical errors corrected; the wording is the author's throughout. The closing invitation to her own mailing list has been kept, since it is part of what she wrote.

body.v: A farmer went out to sow his seed... But the seed on good soil stands for those with a noble and good heart, who hear the word, retain it and by persevering, produce a crop.

It's always very exciting to have the Spirit lead you back into a familiar passage and show you something very fresh and new! In a recent prayer commitment, the Lord directed me to Luke 8 and instructed me to pray through these verses, regarding not the preached word of the Lord, but the prophetic word of the Lord which had been "sown" into our lives, businesses, and nation. I had never considered that before!

The passage came freshly alive, as did the confirmation, that the fulfillment of the prophetic words received from the Lord may have more to do with the heart condition of the hearer than the inherent power of the word. Join me in praying through this passage; allow the Spirit to shift the focus from hope deferred to His grace releasing persevering expectation.
The fulfillment of the prophetic words received from the Lord may have more to do with the heart condition of the hearer than the inherent power of the word.
body.highlight: the heart condition of the hearer

body.v: The prayer

Lord, we thank you for sowing into our lives. As you have spoken prophetically we have heard your desires and plans for our lives, businesses, ministries, and even nations. Stir us afresh to resist your enemy (and ours) from snatching that Word from the pathway that we are on, even when the pathway looks far different than the future landscape of the fulfilled Word.

Lord, at times we are fickle! You speak to us and we respond with joy. But soon the Word "withers". We fail to allow the Word to root in our hearts. Even when the received Word does take root, we do not tend the Word, with faith. We give place and space to "why not" and the Word is displaced by worries, value placed on other things, and even distracting pleasures. We have not cultivated and cleared our lives of what would choke out the prophetic seed sown.
We repent, Lord, and we ask you to cleanse us from our inaccurate allegations against you that you speak but do not fulfill what you say.

Our greatest desire is that your desires will be fulfilled. We align ourselves with even the timing required, to allow the Word, as good seed, to germinate, sprout, and rise up in our view line. We receive the prophetic intentions you have declared. We invite your Spirit to survey the soil of our hearts. We appropriate your grace to work fresh perseverance within us.
We pray that we will be in that number that bear the prophetic Word to completion; and we will see what you have said. We will share in your joy of ripened fruit and a crop of fulfilled Word.
We pray that we will join the ranks of those who have celebrated:
Praise be to the Lord... who with His hands has fulfilled what he promised with his mouth.
Sow more prophetic seed, Lord, until the landscape of our lives, ministries, businesses, and nations becomes a fertile field, bearing much fruit. In Jesus' Name, Amen.

The author invited readers to sign up for Hear the Sound, her regular word of prophetic encouragement, at twosilvertrumpets.ca. That invitation was part of the piece as it appeared in 2013 and is reproduced here; 5Talents has no commercial relationship with Two Silver Trumpets Ministry.

articles.title: A baker in Portland is about to stop serving some of her customers, and it is not about the pastries
articles.deck: They demand more than is reasonable, return products claiming to have found foreign objects, and are never satisfied. Which raises the harder question: why does anyone do business with you?

archiveMeta.editNote: Published as it appeared in the September 2013 issue, page 10. Column reading order repaired and typographical errors corrected; the wording is the author's throughout. Two of the ideas he uses are widely taught rather than his own, and are credited in a note at the foot rather than by altering his text.

body.v: In the town where I live there is a great new European Bakery called "Petite Patisserie". I absolutely love it! One thing is for sure; it has caused me to be very committed to my exercise routine, because otherwise, I'd have to buy a whole new wardrobe of clothes several sizes larger.

I was talking with the owner just recently, about a certain group of people, with whom she is going to stop serving, and for various reasons. They demand more than is reasonable; they return products claiming they found "foreign objects" in them, and they are constantly dissatisfied; in an effort to get things for less or to not pay at all. In short, they lack principles and character.
All of this leads me to ask the question of people with whom I do business. And the answer comes down to a pretty short list. I do business with people I know, like, and trust.
Stop and think about it. I bet you do, too.

So think about this, as a business owner, or one who offers some type of service to others, why do you suppose people do business with you? Initially it is most likely, because you offer some product or service they require. But it is only a matter of time, after they have gotten to know you, that they conclude they either do or do not like you, and most importantly of all, they've determined that they can trust you.
So how do you create trust? How do you become trustworthy? How can your business develop the reputation of being trustworthy? It can be as simple as A, B, and C.
Appreciate your customers

To appreciate something means to raise the value. Mostly this just comes down to great customer service. For example, when a customer walks into your store, your business, or office, how are they greeted? Do they feel valued? Do they feel welcomed? Do they feel appreciated?

Honestly there are places of business that I would never frequent again in my life. Why? Not because of an inferior product, but because of how they made me feel. If I feel ignored, or as if I'm a bother to them, then I won't be a bother any more!
On a deeper level, ask yourself, how does my product or my service raise the value of my customer? How does it meet their need? How does it improve their life?
And it does go both ways. In the case of my bakery owner friend, these "high need customers" must learn to appreciate the high quality product they are receiving.
Be a person of your word

Recently I hired a "professional" to build a water feature in my backyard, a tiny pond with two or three little waterfalls. As time went on and a broken promise was followed by a broken promise, I quickly came to the conclusion that this person is not dependable and whenever he would make another "promise" I would think to myself, "I'll believe it when I see it."

As a person who has to make commitments all the time with my coaching and leadership training company, I've determined that I will never become the person of whom others say, "I'll believe it when I see it."
In order for that not to happen, one of the personal and business values by which I live is, the DWYSYWD principle.
DO WHAT YOU SAY YOU WILL DO! Nothing chips away at the foundation of Trust than empty, broken promises.
body.highlight: DO WHAT YOU SAY YOU WILL DO

body.v: So do you want to grow your business? Do you want to be successful? Do you want others to speak highly of you? It's simple, be a person of your word.
Consistently deliver

How many times would you fly with an airline that advertised 98% of the time we'll get you there safely? Or how many times would you eat in a restaurant that boasted high quality food products most of the time? Or how often would you go back to a Company that once-in-a-while delivered on their product?
The answer is never, never, and never! Why? Because you want, need and expect consistency. So do your customers!

So why should I do business with you? Or maybe the better question is: Why would I do business with you? It's most likely because I've come to know you. I've learned that you are likeable. But most importantly of all, I know I can trust you.
By the way, when you visit me in Portland, I'll be sure to take you to my European Bakery.

Two credits the 2013 page did not carry. Doing business with people you know, like and trust is a formulation long associated with the sales writer Bob Burg. DWYSYWD is from James Kouzes and Barry Posner, who set it out in The Leadership Challenge as the shortest definition of credibility. Both are widely taught in the coaching world the author writes from, and neither is presented here as his own coinage.

articles.title: A missionary was preaching, and I got up and ran out of the service
articles.deck: He knew exactly what God was saying to him, and he did not want it. Then came months of running, which is where he found the book of Jonah useful.

archiveMeta.editNote: Published as it appeared in the September 2013 issue, page 14. Column reading order repaired and typographical errors corrected; the wording is the author's throughout. Pull quotes are drawn from his own sentences.

body.v: But Jonah ran away from the Lord...

Did you ever just outright blow it? Have you messed up so bad that you think you will never get out of a situation? Do you think that God has left you behind and He's moving forward without you? Did you disobey God and get yourself in a bad relationship or bad debt?
I take comfort in the book of Jonah, because I see that I'm not the only one who messes up.

Here was a prophet of God who ran away from God. Yet, the example of Jonah represents our lives many times. God calls us and we run, or we do the opposite of what he says, and we end up engulfed in a "whale" of problems.

Shortly after I was saved, I went to a church service, where a missionary was preaching. Everything that the missionary was saying was piercing my heart. I knew that God was telling me that I was going to be serving Him in Missions. While he was preaching, I literally jumped up out of my seat and ran out of the Service. I thought that there was no way I was going to any foreign country. I too had become a modern day Jonah.
I literally jumped up out of my seat and ran out of the Service. I too had become a modern day Jonah.
The storm
...such a violent storm arose...

When you first turn from God's Will, everything may go smoothly at first, but then suddenly the storms of life start to rock your boat. Your problems start to overwhelm you and your life begins to have an adverse affect on others. You try to tell others that God's in control, but they are fearful of what's happening in your life and abandon you.
But the Lord provided a great fish to swallow Jonah, and Jonah was inside the fish three days and three nights...

Unexpected problems have multiplied and you're totally engulfed in difficulties that are impossible to get out of. You are now riding around in the belly of God's whale, trying to figure out how to get out of your hopeless circumstances. You may have failed God, failed your loved ones, failed yourself, and you feel that it's impossible to get back. I'm sure Jonah wasn't thinking about the distant future while riding in the belly of the whale.
The prayer from inside
From inside the fish Jonah prayed...

Jonah's only concern was to turn back His life to the Author and Finisher of his Faith. He knew he was in "deeper" than he could get out of, and only God could rescue him. Many of us are in such impossible circumstances that only God could get us out and put our feet back on solid ground again. It's when we cry out to Him with a sincere heart and we submit to His Will again that He hears our cries and answers our prayers.

I ran away from God for months shortly after I had ran out of that church Service, and I became a prodigal son. Yet God in His mercy loved me back to Him, and I can now say with a sincere heart that I consider it a honor and a privilege to serve Him in a foreign country.
You are not stuck in the whale

You may think that you failed God's plan so much that you're stuck in the whale for life, but that's not true. Jonah was not the only person who messed up in the Bible. David failed royally as he lied one day and because of his lies all the priests of Nob were murdered. He also committed adultery with Bathsheba and had her husband murdered. Yet the Scriptures tell us that he had a heart after God, and he too cried out to God with a broken and contrite heart.
It does not matter what sin you're committing. God will forgive you and restore you back to the joy of your Salvation (Psalm 51) as long as you confess your sins!
And I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten.

This Scripture tells us that God will restore the years that you lost and will make you usable again for His glory. Despite David's sin, Jesus was a descendent of him. He even used Jonah's failures to represent 3 days of Jonah in the whale, as a comparison of Jesus descending into the ground for three days! So God can turn our failures around and use them for His glory when we seek His will again.
Like Jonah, let our prayer be:

In my distress I called to the Lord, and He answered me. From the depths of the grave I called for help, and You listened to my cry. You hurled me into the deep, into the very heart of the seas, and the currents swirled about me; all Your waves and breakers swept over me. I said, 'I have been banished from Your sight; yet I will look again toward Your holy temple.' The engulfing waters threatened me, the deep surrounded me; seaweeds were wrapped around my head. To the roots of the mountains I sank down; the earth beneath barred me in, forever. But You brought my life up from the pit, O Lord my God. When my life was ebbing away, I remembered You, Lord, and my prayer rose to You, to Your holy temple. Those who cling to worthless idols forfeit the grace that could be theirs. But I, with a song of thanksgiving, will sacrifice to You. What I have vowed I will make good. Salvation comes from the Lord.

articles.title: In thirty years he made one convert, and that convert went on to do more than he did
articles.deck: David Livingstone is the most famous missionary Britain ever produced. By the measure he chose for himself he failed almost completely, and the most remarkable act in his story was performed by men whose names are on no gravestone.

archiveMeta.editNote: The Missionary Story on pages 17 to 19 of the September 2013 issue was reproduced word for word from the entry on Livingstone by R. Grundemann in the New Schaff-Herzog Encyclopedia of Religious Knowledge, published in 1910, and carried Elizabeth Clayton's byline. The text is out of copyright, so this was not theft of property, but it was passed off as ours. This is a new article, researched from primary sources and current scholarship and written in September 2026. Nothing of the 1910 entry survives in it.

body.v: Estimates of how many people David Livingstone converted in thirty years in Africa vary between one and none.

The variation exists because Livingstone wrote off his single convert as a backslider within five months of baptising him. That man was Sechele, kgosi of the BaKwena. At his death in 1892 he ruled about thirty thousand people, most of them Christian, and the historian Neil Parsons of the University of Botswana judges that he did more to spread Christianity in nineteenth-century southern Africa than virtually any single European missionary.
Livingstone's own birthplace museum in Scotland puts it without flinching: his success as a missionary was limited, and Sechele's was not.
Less than a minute at a time
He was born in 1813 at Shuttle Row, mill housing on the Clyde, into one room that at its fullest held seven people. The building held twenty-four families.

At ten he went into the cotton mill as a piecer, ducking under the moving spinning jenny to tie broken threads. The mill ran from six in the morning until eight at night, with forty minutes for breakfast and forty-five for dinner. It had among the longest hours in Scotland.

With part of his first week's wages he bought a Latin grammar. He went to night school from eight until ten, then read at home until midnight or later, in his own words, "if my mother did not interfere by jumping up and snatching the books out of my hands". He had to be back at the machine at six.
He also propped the book on the spinning jenny and read a line each time he passed it. His biographer worked out what that meant in practice.
The utmost interval that Livingstone could have for reading at one time was less than a minute.
body.attr: W. G. Blaikie, on Livingstone reading at the mill

body.v: He knew Virgil and Horace at sixteen. At twenty-three he began at Anderson's University in Glasgow, walking the eight miles in from Blantyre every Monday of term and returning to the mill in the vacations. He qualified in medicine in November 1840 and sailed that December. He had wanted China. The Opium Wars closed it, so he went to southern Africa instead, arriving in March 1841.
One convert, and what it cost him

Sechele was a rainmaker, which in his society was a public office and not a superstition, and he had five wives. Livingstone required him to give up both. It took three years to get to the second, and the baptism came in 1848, during the worst drought anyone could remember.

Livingstone described the town the next morning: "a general consternation seemed to have seized both young and old. The town was as quiet as if it had been a Sunday. Many of the spectators were in tears, but these were in general tears of sorrow for the loss of their rainmaker."

Five months later one of the divorced wives was found to be pregnant. Livingstone's journal records his own reaction, that the news "loosened all my bones", and his decision: "Cut him off for a season." Not excommunicated. Suspended.
What Sechele said in reply is the sentence worth carrying out of this article.
Do not give me up because of this. I shall never give up Jesus. You and I will stand before him together.
body.highlight: I shall never give up Jesus

body.v: The two men last met in 1852. Livingstone spent years calling him an apostate, then a backslider though not an apostate. In a field diary of 1870, twenty-two years after the baptism and alone in central Africa, he wrote: "I solemnly declare that I considered him to be a true Christian. The first extempore prayer he uttered in my presence could not have been learned but from the Holy Spirit."

By then Sechele had been leading services himself for two decades. When the first British missionaries reached the Ndebele in 1859 they found people already holding Christian prayers. Sechele had got there first.
The expedition that was recalled
Livingstone resigned from the London Missionary Society in 1857. His book had made him wealthy and famous, and the Society would not fund work that was not direct evangelism.

What followed was the Zambezi expedition, planned for two years, funded with five thousand pounds of government money, and lasting six and a half. The rapids he had promised were navigable turned out to be impassable at any water level, which he discovered only after making the promise. The steam launch burned tons of hardwood a day, choked on its own ash, and was nicknamed the Asthmatic. His expedition doctor wrote that he could come to no other conclusion than that Livingstone was out of his mind and a most unsafe leader. He dismissed two of his best men on charges that did not stand up, and never gave one of them a hearing.

In April 1862 his wife Mary died of malaria at Shupanga, aged forty-one. She had been born in Africa, spoke Tswana fluently, and was well enough known in southern Africa that he was sometimes introduced as her husband. In eighteen years of marriage they had spent eight in each other's company. His journal: "For the first time in my life I feel willing to die." His published account of the expedition says almost nothing about it.

The Foreign Office recalled the expedition in 1863. The Times: "We were promised cotton, sugar, and indigo, and of course we get none. We were promised converts to the gospel, and not a one has been made."
The market at Nyangwe

On 15 July 1871, at a market village on the Lualaba, Livingstone watched armed men open fire on a crowd of two to three thousand people, most of them women. He had left the market minutes before it started. A second party fired on those running for the canoes. He counted seventeen villages burning that day and six the next. The dead were put at between four and five hundred, a figure he was careful to attribute to the traders themselves rather than to his own count.

His field diary that day says: "It is awful, terrible." The next: "Hell without the fire and brimstone." He had been writing for months in ink improvised from berries and cloth dye. To record this he switched to his last reserve of proper iron gall ink, so that the words would not fade.

Four months later Henry Stanley found him at Ujiji and carried out a letter describing the massacre. Published in 1872, it was the only account of Nyangwe to appear in Livingstone's lifetime, and it landed, as the historian Dorothy Helly puts it, in the middle of a well-planned campaign already under way to end the seaborne slave trade.

He died on 1 May 1873. Five weeks later the Sultan of Zanzibar signed a treaty closing the slave market there. The link is usually drawn as cause and effect and it will not bear that weight: the British envoy had already been refused once in January, and the signature was finally obtained under an explicit threat of naval blockade. The market closed. Slavery in Zanzibar was not abolished for another quarter century.
The part that is not his
He died at Chitambo's village in what is now Zambia, in the small hours, and the men with him then did something that has no obvious parallel.

They buried his heart under a tree. They dried and salted the body, bent the legs back to shorten it, wrapped it in calico and bark and tarred sailcloth, and carried it about a thousand miles to the coast, walking for nine months. One community refused them passage for carrying human remains. When a British relief expedition met them and urged them to bury it, they refused and kept walking.

Two men led that march. Abdullah Susi was from Shupanga and had joined the Zambezi expedition as a woodcutter; he built the stretcher that carried Livingstone at the end, and carved his name into the bark of the burial tree. James Chuma had been freed from a slave caravan by Livingstone in 1861, aged about eleven.
Why this belongs in an Indian magazine
Because of where those men were educated.

Chuma sailed to India with Livingstone and spent 1864 and 1865 at a school in Bombay. Jacob Wainwright, who kept the only handwritten eyewitness account of Livingstone's death, had been enslaved as a boy near Kilwa, freed by a British ship, brought to Bombay at seven or eight, and schooled by the Church Missionary Society at Nasik. The Royal Geographical Society calls this group the Bombay Africans. At least thirty of them are identifiable.
Before they sailed, they were told plainly what the job was: if he were dead, they must find his grave and bring back his bones.

Wainwright walked in the funeral procession at Westminster Abbey and threw a palm branch into the grave. Chuma and Susi reached England after the funeral was over. The gravestone reads BROUGHT BY FAITHFUL HANDS OVER LAND AND SEA. It is the only mention of them, and it names nobody.
The honest criticism

In 1857 at Cambridge, Livingstone told an audience he was going back to Africa to make an open path for commerce and Christianity, and asked them to carry out the work he had begun. He believed legitimate trade would drive out the slave trade. The idea was not originally his and the consequences were not what he pictured.

The first Commissioner of the British Central Africa Protectorate wrote in 1891 that Livingstone's work was nearing the fruition he longed for, under the flag he loved. The town of Livingstone in Zambia was founded by Cecil Rhodes's company, and its museum was called the Rhodes-Livingstone Museum until 1966. Fidelis Nkomazana of the University of Botswana puts it as fairly as it can be put: the drive to open Africa did contribute to European imperialism, but it would be wrong to say Livingstone consciously promoted it.

Against that, said with equal plainness: he had no patience with the racial theories then hardening across Europe and America, wrote about the "stupid prejudice against colour", and argued that slavery produced racial contempt rather than the reverse. He attacked Boer treatment of Africans from the day he arrived and paid for it. He was also capable of worse than inconsistency. In 1871, having failed to buy a canoe from a chief called Kalenga, he sent his men to flog him, and then cut the episode to a few sentences in the version he prepared for publication.
So what, in 2026?

Livingstone's life does not work as an argument for going somewhere far away and succeeding. He went, and by the terms he set himself he failed: one convert, one expedition recalled, a wife buried on a riverbank, and, in his own words, "we were made the unwilling instruments of extending the slave trade".

What survived him was not the plan. It was a chief in Botswana who took the thing seriously enough to keep it after the missionary gave up on him, and thirty thousand people who heard it from Sechele rather than from Livingstone. It was two men schooled in Bombay and Nasik who walked a thousand miles with a body because they had said they would.

Museums in Scotland now hang the questions on the wall rather than the answers: he accepted help from slave traders, so why is he remembered as an abolitionist? He is called a hero in books and films and in his own writing, so who are the other heroes of this story? Those are good questions to put to a famous man, and better ones to put to yourself.

Sources: Livingstone Online, the scholarly edition of his manuscripts, including the 1871 Field Diary and the spectral imaging project; the David Livingstone Birthplace Museum; the One More Voice project, which publishes Jacob Wainwright's own account and Sechele's record; W. G. Blaikie, The Personal Life of David Livingstone (1880); Neil Parsons, King Khama, Emperor Joe, and the Great White Queen (1998); Dorothy O. Helly, Livingstone's Legacy (1987); Joanna Lewis, Empire of Sentiment (2018); Fidelis Nkomazana, University of Botswana; the Royal Geographical Society on the Bombay Africans; and Westminster Abbey. Byline: this column is written by Elizabeth Clayton.
